```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
arizona_weather <- read_csv("data/arizona_weather.csv")

# Hot days and freeze nights per year at each station
yearly <- arizona_weather |>
  group_by(station_name, year) |>
  summarise(
    hot_days = sum(tmax_f >= 100, na.rm = TRUE),
    freeze_nights = sum(tmin_f <= 32, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
tucson  <- filter(yearly, str_detect(station_name, "Tucson"))
phoenix <- filter(yearly, str_detect(station_name, "Phoenix"))
flagstaff <- filter(yearly, str_detect(station_name, "Flagstaff"))

# Tucson winters run from July 1 to June 30 (complete winters: 1982-83 to 2023-24)
tucson_winters <- arizona_weather |>
  filter(str_detect(station_name, "Tucson"), tmin_f <= 32) |>
  mutate(winter = if_else(month >= 7, year, year - 1)) |>
  filter(winter %in% 1982:2023) |>
  group_by(winter) |>
  summarise(freeze_nights = n(), first_freeze = min(date))
```

## Project goal

We will show how the start, end, and length of the hot season and the freeze season changed from 1982 to 2024, using one season calendar drawn for Tucson, Phoenix, and Flagstaff, and we will check whether the mild windows between the two seasons move together across the three cities. While doing this, we will teach ourselves to color-label charts with the `ggtext` package.

## Goals and motivation

Many decisions in Arizona depend on dates and not on yearly averages. The University of Arizona Cooperative Extension's March gardening guide for Pima County advises gardeners to watch for the last local frost and to plant early enough for vegetables to mature before the heat of June. The last freeze in spring and the first 100°F day mark the edges of a mild planting window, and the last 100°F day and the first freeze mark a second window in fall. A yearly average cannot show either window, because two years can have the same average while their freezes end weeks apart.

As students living in Tucson, we want to see how those edges have moved. We include Phoenix and Flagstaff because each city has its own windows: Phoenix is shaped mostly by heat, Flagstaff mostly by cold, and Tucson by both. Drawing the same chart for all three tells us whether a change is shared across Arizona or local to one place.

## Dataset

**Source :** We use daily weather records from NOAA's Global Historical Climatology Network - Daily (GHCN-Daily), downloaded from NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information on November 6, 2026, in degrees Fahrenheit. The data is available at [NOAA GHCN-Daily](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/products/land-based-station/global-historical-climatology-network-daily).

**Why we chose it :** It is an official, documented source with long daily records, and our question needs only the daily high and low temperature at each station. It also includes three airport stations at very different elevations, which lets us compare cities.

**Size :** The cleaned file, `data/arizona_weather.csv`, has `r format(nrow(arizona_weather), big.mark = ",")` rows and `r ncol(arizona_weather)` columns. Each row is one day at one of `r n_distinct(arizona_weather$station_name)` airport stations. Each station has `r format(nrow(arizona_weather) / n_distinct(arizona_weather$station_name), big.mark = ",")` rows, one for every day from `r min(arizona_weather$year)` to `r max(arizona_weather$year)`.

**Missing values :** Days with no reading are kept as `NA`. There are `r sum(is.na(arizona_weather$tmax_f))` missing daily highs and `r sum(is.na(arizona_weather$tmin_f))` missing daily lows.

**Left out :** We also downloaded Yuma, but its record ends in June 1996, which is too short to study change over time, so we dropped it.

```{r}
#| label: station-table
#| echo: false
arizona_weather |>
  group_by(station_name, station_id) |>
  summarise(
    rows = n(),
    missing_highs = sum(is.na(tmax_f)),
    missing_lows = sum(is.na(tmin_f)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Station", "NOAA ID", "Rows", "Missing highs", "Missing lows"),
    format.args = list(big.mark = ",")
  )
```

**Variables :**

| Variable | Type | Description |
|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|
| `station_id` | character | NOAA station ID |
| `station_name` | character | Name of the weather station |
| `date` | date | Date of the observation |
| `tmax_f` | number | Highest temperature of the day (°F) |
| `tmin_f` | number | Lowest temperature of the day (°F) |
| `year` | number | Calendar year of the date |
| `month` | number | Month of the date (1 to 12) |
| `season` | character | "summer" (June to August), "winter" (December to February), or "other" |
| `season_year` | number | Year the season is counted in (December is counted with the next January and February) |

Our analysis uses `station_name`, `date`, `tmax_f`, `tmin_f`, `year`, and `month`. The `season` and `season_year` columns were made during cleaning and are not needed for this question.

## Research question

From 1982 to 2024, how did the start, end, and length of the hot season (days with a high of 100°F or more) and the freeze season (nights with a low of 32°F or less) change in Tucson, Phoenix, and Flagstaff, and do the spring window (last freeze to first 100°F day) and the fall window (last 100°F day to the next first freeze) grow, shrink, or shift together across the three cities?

**Why we chose it :** Planting and plant-protection decisions depend on when the hazards begin and end, which averages hide. Putting heat and cold in one question lets us study the windows between them, and comparing three cities shows whether a change is regional or local. The question is for gardeners and the programs that advise them, with Tucson as our lead example.

**What we expect :** We expect the first 100°F day to move earlier and the last to move later in Tucson and Phoenix, and the last spring freeze to move earlier and the first fall freeze to move later in Tucson and Flagstaff. We do not yet know how large any change is.

### Why 100°F and 32°F

Both cutoffs come from established local and national practice. The National Weather Service office in Tucson publishes yearly counts of 100°F days going back to 1895, and 32°F is the freezing point of water and the temperature the National Weather Service uses in its definition of a freeze. As a check on our data, the most 100°F days in a Tucson year in our file is `r max(tucson$hot_days)` in `r tucson$year[which.max(tucson$hot_days)]`, which matches the National Weather Service record of 112 days in 2024. We call a night at or below 32°F a "freeze night", which is a simpler working definition than the official one. These cutoffs are conventions, so we will also test nearby values (105°F, 95°F, and 28°F) to see whether our conclusions change.

### Do the data support the question?

Tucson has `r min(tucson$hot_days)` to `r max(tucson$hot_days)` days a year at 100°F or more and `r min(tucson$freeze_nights)` to `r max(tucson$freeze_nights)` freeze nights a year, so both seasons have enough events to compare across decades. In `r nrow(tucson_winters)` of the 42 complete winters (July 1982 to June 2024) Tucson had at least one freeze night, with a median of `r median(tucson_winters$freeze_nights)` per winter. In `r sum(month(tucson_winters$first_freeze) <= 6)` of those winters the first freeze came in January or later, which is why we define a winter as July 1 to June 30 and never split a freeze season at New Year's Day.

Phoenix reaches 100°F on at least `r min(phoenix$hot_days)` days every year, but only `r sum(phoenix$freeze_nights > 0)` of its `r nrow(phoenix)` years have any freeze night. Flagstaff has `r min(flagstaff$freeze_nights)` to `r max(flagstaff$freeze_nights)` freeze nights a year, but at most `r max(flagstaff$hot_days)` days at 100°F or more. So Phoenix has only a heat edge and Flagstaff only a freeze edge, and we report that as a result, not as missing data. We keep the same cutoffs in all three cities so the charts can be compared directly.

## Analysis plan

**How we will answer it.**

1.  For each city and calendar year, find the first and last day with a high of 100°F or more.
2.  For each city and winter (July 1 to June 30), find the first and last freeze night.
3.  Calculate the hot season, the freeze season, and the spring and fall windows in days, from the actual dates. A season is the span from its first to its last event, and a window is the number of days strictly between two events.
4.  Compare the early years (1982-1991) with the recent years (2015-2024) using medians, and estimate the trend in each event date in days per decade.
5.  Mark years with missing readings near an event, and check whether leaving them out changes the trends.
6.  Repeat the key results with the nearby cutoffs (105°F, 95°F, and 28°F).

**Variables involved:** `station_name`, `date`, `year`, `month`, `tmax_f`, and `tmin_f`.

**Variables to be created:** `winter` (the July-to-June year), the first and last 100°F day, the first and last freeze night of each winter, and the length of each season and window.

**External data to be merged in:** none.

## Visualization plan

**Main chart: a season calendar for each city :**There are three panels side by side (Flagstaff, Tucson, Phoenix, from coldest to hottest) that share the same axes. Each row is one year, with 1982 at the top, and each tile is one day from January to December. Orange marks days of 100°F or more, blue marks freeze nights, light gray marks everything else, and missing readings stay blank. We add a thin trend line only for an event that happens in nearly every year, so Phoenix gets no freeze lines and Flagstaff gets no heat lines. Reading down a panel shows how the windows changed over time, and reading across the panels shows whether the cities move together.

**Supporting chart: event dates by city :** Four small panels, one for each event (first 100°F day, last 100°F day, last freeze of the winter, and first freeze of the next winter), show one dot per year with a trend line labeled in days per decade. Only the cities that have each event appear in its panel. This chart shows how big the shifts are, which the calendar alone cannot show.

**What we will teach ourselves :** We will learn the `ggtext` package, which was not covered in class. We will use it to color the words "hot day" and "freeze night" in the subtitle to match the tiles, so the subtitle works as the legend, and to label the spring and fall windows directly on the chart. We will confirm with Professor Leach that this counts as new material, and we will keep short learning notes in the repository.

## Limitations

- The 100°F and 32°F cutoffs are conventions, and the freeze night is a single-station version of the official definition.
- Three airport stations do not represent all of Arizona.
- Flagstaff has some missing readings, and we will mark any years where they sit near an event.
- Our data ends on December 31, 2024, so the 2024-25 winter is incomplete and will be marked as not yet observed.
- A peer suggested that concrete and buildings may lengthen Phoenix's heat season. We can compare how long the hot season lasts in each city, but we cannot separate urban heat from regional climate with this data, so we will describe the pattern without claiming a cause.
